scenes.title: What Counts as an Outlier
scenes.description: Three kinds of anomaly, three regimes of supervision, and the one honest admission every detector has to make: the threshold is a decision, not a discovery.
scenes.markdown:
# What counts as an outlier

Before any algorithm, a definition — and the definition is the hard part.

Hawkins, 1980: *an outlier is an observation which deviates so much from the other observations as to arouse suspicions that it was generated by a different mechanism.* Every detector in this lesson is an attempt to make **"deviates so much"** computable. None of them can tell you what to do about a point once it is flagged; that part is yours.

## Three kinds

| Kind | What is wrong | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Point** | The value itself is extreme | A single \$4,000,000 transaction |
| **Contextual** | The value is fine, the context is not | 25 °C — in Helsinki, in January |
| **Collective** | Every value is fine, the *sequence* is not | A heartbeat that flatlines at a normal voltage |

The first is what people picture. The second and third are where the money is, and neither is visible to a rule that looks at one number at a time.

## Three regimes of supervision

- **Unsupervised** — no labels at all. You assume anomalies are rare and different, and you rank. This is the usual case, and every method in scenes 2–5 is one of these.
- **Semi-supervised (one-class)** — you have data you *believe* is clean. Fit the normal, flag departures. Often the most honest framing of a real problem.
- **Supervised** — you have labels for both classes. Then this is not anomaly detection, it is **imbalanced classification**, and you should reach for a classifier. The benchmark literature is blunt about this: a little supervision beats a lot of architecture.

## The word that ruins everything: *contamination*

Unsupervised methods are fitted on the data they are asked to judge — anomalies included. So the model of "normal" is built partly out of the abnormal. Every failure in scene 2 is a version of this.

> **The data in this lesson is synthetic and seeded.** The anomalies were planted on purpose so that ground truth exists and the detectors can be scored honestly. The *scoring* is real — every number on screen is the published definition, recomputed live.
scenes.prompt: Opening scene of a six-scene lesson on outlier detection. Its job is definitional, not algorithmic: the student should leave knowing (1) point vs contextual vs collective anomalies, (2) unsupervised vs one-class vs supervised, (3) that contamination — fitting the model of normal on data that contains the abnormal — is the structural problem the rest of the lesson keeps running into. Do not teach any specific detector here; scenes 2 to 6 do that. The two visuals are a 2-D cloud with twelve planted point anomalies, and a 128-sample signal with a nine-sample stretch whose values stay inside the global range but whose SHAPE is wrong — that second one is the collective anomaly, and its whole purpose is to be invisible to a z-score. If the student asks why the flat stretch is anomalous when nothing is out of range, that is exactly the right question and the answer is scene 5. The data is seeded and the anomalies were planted; say so if asked. Hawkins' 1980 definition is the one quoted.

steps.title: Which of these does not belong?
steps.description:
192 measurements of two quantities. Some of them were generated by a different mechanism. Before reading on: **which ones, and how sure are you?**

Notice that the question already contains three assumptions — that anomalies are *rare*, that they are *different*, and that "different" means *far away in this particular coordinate system*. Every one of those can fail.
steps.prompt: Eyeball step: the student sees 192 points and no method. Resist naming the planted indices. If they guess, engage with the guess -- the useful realisation is that reasonable people disagree about the borderline points, which is exactly why every detector outputs a RANKING and someone else picks the cut. The three assumptions named in the step text (rare, different, different-in-THESE-coordinates) each get attacked later: rarity in scene 6 via base rate, 'different' in scene 3 via local density, and the coordinate system in scene 3 via Mahalanobis and in scene 5 via learned representations.

steps.title: Contextual and collective — the cases that matter
steps.description:
A different measurement: one quantity, 128 samples, clearly seasonal.

Samples **74–82** are highlighted. Every one of those values is **inside the global range** — none is a record high or a record low, and no rule that examines one sample at a time will ever flag them. What is wrong is that the *shape* stops. The season flattens.

That is a **collective anomaly**: the individual observations are unremarkable and the subsequence is not. Detecting it requires a model of the structure, which is scene 5.
steps.prompt: The collective anomaly. The student must come away certain of one fact: samples 74 to 82 run 10.94 to 11.67 while the whole signal runs 5.39 to 13.89, so the largest |z| inside the window is below 3 and NO per-sample rule flags it. If they ask how to detect it, name the two honest routes -- model the structure and look at the residual (scene 5), or compare the subsequence against every other subsequence (the matrix profile). A contextual anomaly is the neighbouring idea: same value, wrong context, like 25 degrees in a Helsinki January.

info.title: Three kinds
info.content:
**Point** — the value is extreme.

**Contextual** — the value is normal, the context is not.

**Collective** — every value is normal, the *sequence* is not. ← *this one*

The planted window sits entirely inside the global range. Its largest $|z|$ is **below 3**.

steps.title: How much do you know? Three regimes
steps.description:
Which methods are even available to you is decided before you pick one, by what labels you have.

**Unsupervised.** No labels. Assume rare and different; produce a *ranking*; cut it somewhere. Scenes 2–5.

**Semi-supervised / one-class.** You have data you believe is clean. Fit the normal region, flag anything outside. Usually the most honest description of a real problem — you know what last quarter looked like, you do not have a labelled catalogue of frauds.

**Supervised.** Labels for both classes. This is *imbalanced classification*, not anomaly detection, and you should treat it as such. The large public benchmarks are unambiguous here: across 30 algorithms and 57 datasets, no unsupervised method wins everywhere, and even a handful of labels beats a more elaborate unsupervised model.

The practical consequence: **before choosing an algorithm, go and look for labels.** Thirty labelled examples change which half of this lesson applies to you.
steps.prompt: The supervision axis. The single most actionable sentence in the whole lesson lives here: before choosing an algorithm, go and look for labels, because thirty labelled examples change which half of the lesson applies. Cite ADBench honestly -- 30 algorithms, 57 datasets, no unsupervised method wins everywhere, and modest supervision beats elaborate unsupervised architecture. If the student has labels for both classes, tell them plainly that they have an imbalanced classification problem and should use a classifier with PR-AUC as the metric, not an anomaly detector.

steps.title: The structural problem: contamination
steps.description:
Here is the bind that makes unsupervised anomaly detection genuinely hard, and it is not about which algorithm you pick.

You fit a model of *normal* on the data you are about to judge. That data contains the anomalies. So the anomalies participate in defining what normal means — and the more of them there are, or the more extreme they are, the more they drag the definition toward themselves.

A detector that is fooled by exactly the thing it is looking for. Scene 2 shows the simplest possible version, with arithmetic you can do by hand, and it is worse than you would guess.

**What to carry forward.** Three questions to ask of any detector, in this order:
1. What is its model of *normal*, and can contamination move it?
2. What does it output — a hard label, or a score you still have to cut?
3. At your base rate, what does that cut cost you? *(scene 6)*
steps.prompt: The closing frame, and the hinge into scene 2. Contamination: the model of normal is fitted on data that contains the abnormal, so the abnormal helps define normal. Do not let this stay abstract -- scene 2 makes it arithmetic a student can do by hand, where eight bad readings out of sixty drag the mean and the standard deviation so far that the 3-sigma rule catches only two of the eight it was built to catch. The three questions listed are the lesson's through-line; a student who can ask them of an unfamiliar detector has got what the lesson is for.

info.title: The bind
info.content:
Fit normal on data that contains the abnormal, and the abnormal helps define normal.

scenes.title: Statistical Baselines — z-score, MAD, Tukey — and Why They Break
scenes.description: The three-sigma rule, Tukey's fences and the modified z-score on sixty readings — and the moment the first one stops working, with the arithmetic on screen.
scenes.markdown:
# Statistical baselines, and why they break

Sixty readings of one metric. Three rules, all of which you could apply in a spreadsheet.

| Rule | Flag when | Estimator of centre | Estimator of scale |
|---|---|---|---|
| **$k$-sigma / z-score** | $\lvert v - \bar{v}\rvert > k s$ | mean $\bar{v}$ | sd $s$ |
| **Modified z-score** | $\lvert v - \tilde{v}\rvert > k \cdot 1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD}$ | median $\tilde{v}$ | $1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD}$ |
| **Tukey's fences** | $v < Q_1 - 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$ or $v > Q_3 + 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$ | — | IQR |

They look interchangeable. They are not, and the difference is not subtle.

## Breakdown point

The **breakdown point** of an estimator is the smallest fraction of the sample you must corrupt to move it arbitrarily far.

- Mean: $1/n \to 0$. **One** point sent to infinity takes the mean with it.
- Standard deviation: also $0$, and worse — it moves *quadratically* in the corrupted value.
- Median: $1/2$. You must corrupt **half** the sample.
- MAD: $1/2$.

A rule built on a zero-breakdown estimator is a rule the outliers get a vote in.

## Masking and swamping

- **Masking** — outliers inflate the scale estimate until they fall inside their own fence. The rule stops seeing them.
- **Swamping** — the same inflation pushes good points outside the *other* fence.

Both are visible on this screen within three drags of the contamination slider.

## The hypothesis-test framing

**Grubbs' test** asks whether the single most extreme point is too extreme for a normal sample of this size, via $G = \max_i \lvert v_i - \bar{v}\rvert / s$. **Generalized ESD** repeats it for up to $r$ outliers with a corrected critical value. Both assume normality, both inherit the mean and sd, and so both are masked by exactly the contamination they are hunting. Their real contribution is the discipline of asking *how surprising is this under a stated null*, which is a question the machine-learning methods in scenes 3–5 never answer.
scenes.prompt: Scene 2 of six. One dataset: 60 readings ~ N(50, 3), with a `contam` slider that replaces 0 to 8 of them with large values from a fixed list in a fixed order. Three rules are drawn: the k-sigma z-rule (blue, built on mean and sd), the modified z-score (green, built on median and 1.4826*MAD) and Tukey's fences (amber, built on quartiles). The scene has ONE argument and it is arithmetic, not opinion: as contamination rises the mean and sd absorb the outliers, the blue fences run away, and at contam = 8 the 3-sigma rule flags only 2 of the 8 planted readings while the MAD rule flags all 8. Six of the eight planted readings are MISSED by the z-rule -- readings 7, 12, 23, 41, 48 and 55. That is masking. The mean has been dragged from 49.71 to 53.50 and the sd from 2.97 to 10.63, while the median moved 49.65 to 50.34 and 1.4826*MAD moved 3.41 to 3.88. Every number on screen is computed live from the actual definitions. If the student asks why 1.4826, the proof panel derives it: 1/Phi^{-1}(0.75). If they ask which rule to use in practice, the honest answer is the robust one by default, and a hypothesis test only when normality is genuinely plausible and you need a stated false-positive rate.

steps.title: Sixty readings of one metric
steps.description:
Sixty measurements of something that is supposed to be stable. The contamination slider is at **0**: this is the clean sample, and it really is clean — every reading was drawn from the same normal distribution.

steps.title: The three-sigma rule
steps.description:
Two blue lines at $\bar{v} \pm k s$. Anything outside is flagged.

With $k = 3$ and clean normal data this should flag about $0.27\%$ of readings — which over sixty readings means **it should flag nothing**, and it doesn't. So far the rule is behaving exactly as advertised.

Drag $k$ to see the fence move. Notice that even here the rule already has a hidden assumption baked in: it is calibrated to the normal distribution, and $k = 3$ only means "$0.27\%$" if the data really is normal. On a heavy-tailed metric — latency, transaction size, almost anything in a real system — three sigma flags far more than you budgeted for.
steps.prompt: Introduce the k-sigma rule and its normal-distribution calibration. Two things to land: (1) k = 3 corresponds to 0.27% two-sided ONLY under normality, and most operational metrics are heavy-tailed, so the practical false-positive rate is much higher than the budget implies; (2) the rule is still working correctly here, which is the necessary setup for it failing in the next step. Do not jump ahead to masking yet.

add.prompt: The z-rule's fences: mean plus and minus k standard deviations, with the mean itself drawn faintly between them. Blue is the colour of the non-robust family throughout this lesson. Both fences and the centre line are live expressions, so they move the instant either slider moves. The right-hand blue axis relabels the SAME rows as the left one in units of the classical z-score, (v - mean)/sd; nothing is plotted against it, so the two scales cannot disagree about where a reading sits. It is recomputed live, so as contamination inflates sd the z axis compresses and a reading that was 4 sigma out slides toward 2.

steps.title: Now add the outliers it was built to catch
steps.description:
Drag **contamination** up from 0, one reading at a time, and watch the blue fences.

They run away. Each outlier you add pulls the mean up and inflates the standard deviation — and the fence is *defined* in terms of that inflated standard deviation, so the fence retreats past the very reading that inflated it.

At **contamination = 8** the arithmetic is: the mean has moved from $49.71$ to $53.50$ and the standard deviation from $2.97$ to $10.63$. A $3\sigma$ fence sits above $85$. Six of the eight planted readings are now **inside** it.

This is **masking**, and it is not a corner case — it is what a zero-breakdown estimator does by construction.
steps.prompt: The core failure. Get the student to drag the slider themselves rather than reading the numbers off the panel. The mechanism must be stated as a loop, not as a fact: an outlier inflates s, the fence is defined in terms of s, so the fence moves out past the outlier. At contam = 8 the mean is 53.50 and the sd is 10.63, so the upper 3-sigma fence sits at about 85.4, and readings 7, 12, 23, 41, 48 and 55 (values 72, 85, 78, 69, 67, 74) all fall below it -- six of the eight planted readings, missed. Only 30 and 3 (values 92 and 88) survive the fence. This is masking. Swamping is the mirror image and is worth naming: the same inflation can push the LOWER fence down past good readings, which on other datasets produces false positives at the opposite tail.

steps.title: Swap in estimators the outliers cannot move
steps.description:
Two green lines at $\tilde{v} \pm k \cdot 1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD}$ — the median, and the median absolute deviation from the median.

They barely move. Between contamination 0 and 8 the median travels from $49.65$ to $50.34$ and $1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD}$ from $3.41$ to $3.88$, because to move a median you have to corrupt half the sample, and eight of sixty is not half.

**Why $1.4826$?** Because MAD on its own is not an estimate of $\sigma$ — it is an estimate of $\sigma\,\Phi^{-1}(0.75) \approx 0.6745\,\sigma$. Dividing by that, i.e. multiplying by $1/\Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 1.4826$, makes the two scales comparable so that the same $k$ means the same thing in both rules. The proof panel derives it.

This is the single highest-value swap in the whole lesson: same rule, same $k$, two different estimators, and one of them keeps working.
steps.prompt: The fix, and the derivation of 1.4826. Emphasise that nothing about the RULE changed -- it is still 'flag anything more than k scale units from the centre'. Only the estimators changed, and that was enough. The breakdown-point framing is the general principle: the mean and sd have breakdown 0, the median and MAD have breakdown 1/2. The proof panel derives 1.4826 = 1/Phi^{-1}(0.75) from the definition of MAD under normality, and argues both breakdown points. If the student asks about other robust scale estimators, Qn and Sn (Rousseeuw and Croux) are more efficient than MAD at the same breakdown point, and trimmed or Winsorized statistics are the cruder cousins.

steps.title: Masking, counted
steps.description:
The two rules, plotted against contamination. The grey diagonal is the truth — $c$ planted readings at contamination $c$. A perfect rule would sit on it.

The **green** line tracks the diagonal: the MAD rule finds every planted reading, all the way to eight.

The **blue** line climbs to three and then turns around and comes back down. Adding more outliers makes the $k\sigma$ rule find *fewer* of them. By eight it is catching two.

A detector whose performance is a non-monotone function of how much there is to detect is not a detector you can reason about.
steps.prompt: The summary picture, and the most quotable fact in the scene: the blue curve is NON-MONOTONE. It rises to 3 and then falls back to 2 as contamination climbs to 8, meaning more anomalies make the rule find fewer of them. The green curve sits on the diagonal throughout. Tukey's fences (amber) also track it well -- quartiles have breakdown 1/4, which is less than the median's 1/2 but far more than the mean's 0, and 8 of 60 is under a quarter. steps.title: Tukey's fences, and the tests you were taught
steps.description:
**Tukey's fences** — $Q_1 - 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$ and $Q_3 + 1.5\,\mathrm{IQR}$, the whiskers on every box plot you have ever seen — are the amber line above. They hold up here because quartiles have breakdown point $1/4$: better than the mean's $0$, worse than the median's $1/2$. Push contamination past a quarter of the sample and they break too.

The $1.5$ is a convention, not a derivation. Under normality the fences sit at about $\pm 2.7\sigma$ and flag roughly $0.7\%$ of clean data.

**Grubbs' test** turns the largest $z$ into a hypothesis test: reject normality's claim on the most extreme point when $G = \max_i \lvert v_i - \bar{v} \rvert / s$ exceeds a critical value depending on $n$ and $\alpha$. Right now $G = ${{toFixed(adGrubbs(contam), 3)}}$. Watch what it does as contamination rises — it goes **down**, for exactly the reason the blue fence went up.

**Generalized ESD** runs Grubbs up to $r$ times with a corrected critical value, which fixes the "only one outlier" limitation but not the masking, because it is still built on the mean and the sd.

## What to take from this scene

1. Robust estimators by default. The swap costs one line of code.
2. Check the **breakdown point** of anything you rely on.
3. A rule calibrated under normality gives you a known false-positive rate *only* if the data is normal.
4. Every method in the rest of this lesson has a version of this same problem — it is fitted on data that includes what it is looking for. The good ones are explicit about it.
steps.prompt: Closing step. Three things to land. (1) Tukey's 1.5 is a convention, not a theorem -- under normality the fences land near 2.7 sigma and flag about 0.7%. A hypothesis test built on non-robust estimators is masked exactly like the rule it formalises. (3) The generalisation forward: every later method also fits its model of normal on contaminated data, and the difference between a good method and a bad one is whether it is explicit about that. Scene 3 begins by breaking a different assumption -- not robustness, but the idea that one global notion of 'far' applies everywhere in the data.

proof.title: Why 1.4826 — the MAD consistency constant — and why the median survives
proof.techniqueHint: Two independent arguments: one calibrates MAD against σ under normality, the other counts how many points it takes to break each estimator.
proof.goal: Show that $1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD}$ is a consistent estimator of $\sigma$ for normal data, and that the mean has breakdown point $0$ while the median has breakdown point $1/2$.
proof.prompt: The proof behind scene 2's fix. Two halves, deliberately: the first is a calibration (why the magic constant is what it is), the second is the reason the swap works at all (breakdown point). Students often think 1.4826 is an empirical fudge factor; it is exactly 1/Phi^{-1}(0.75), a consequence of the normal quantile function and nothing else. Note the honest caveat in the last step: consistency for sigma is a NORMALITY result, and MAD's robustness is not -- MAD stays robust on any distribution, it just stops estimating that distribution's sigma.

steps.justification: $\lvert X - \mu\rvert / \sigma$ is half-normal, and $P(\lvert Z \rvert \le z) = 2\Phi(z) - 1$. Setting that to $\tfrac12$ gives $\Phi(z) = 0.75$, so the median of $\lvert Z \rvert$ is $\Phi^{-1}(0.75)$.
steps.explanation: The median of the *absolute* deviation is the $75$th percentile of the underlying normal, because folding the distribution at $\mu$ maps the upper half onto $[0, \infty)$ and halves every tail probability.

nodes.description: σ — the scale we actually want

steps.label: So rescale by the reciprocal of that quantile
steps.justification: The sample MAD converges in probability to the population median absolute deviation, and that equals $\sigma \Phi^{-1}(0.75)$ by the previous line.
steps.explanation: There is nothing empirical about $1.4826$. It is a normal quantile, to as many digits as you care to print: $\Phi^{-1}(0.75) = 0.6744897501960817$, so the constant is $1.482602218505602$.

steps.label: Breakdown point
steps.justification: The supremum runs over every sample $V'$ obtained from $V$ by replacing $m$ of its $n$ points with arbitrary values.
steps.explanation: In words: the smallest fraction of the sample an adversary must control to move your estimator as far as they like.

steps.label: The mean breaks at one point
steps.justification: Replacing a single observation $v_1$ by $c$ shifts the mean by $(c - v_1)/n$, which is unbounded in $c$.
steps.explanation: The standard deviation is worse still: the same substitution moves $s$ like $\lvert c \rvert / \sqrt{n}$, so a single corrupted reading inflates the *scale* without bound — and it is the scale that defines the fence.

steps.label: The median needs half the sample

half.label: breakdown ½ — the best any translation-equivariant estimator can do

steps.justification: With fewer than $n/2$ points corrupted, at least one uncorrupted observation remains on each side of the median, so the order statistic in the middle is still bracketed by real data and stays bounded.
steps.explanation: And $1/2$ is optimal: no translation-equivariant estimator of location can exceed it, because at exactly half an adversary can present two equally valid samples that disagree.

steps.label: Same rule, different estimators
steps.justification: By the calibration, the right-hand side means the same thing as $k s$ on clean normal data; by the breakdown argument, it goes on meaning it under contamination.
steps.explanation: One honest caveat. Consistency for $\sigma$ is a **normality** result: on a heavy-tailed or skewed metric, $1.4826\,\mathrm{MAD}$ is still robust but is no longer estimating that distribution's standard deviation, and $k$ no longer buys you a known false-positive rate. Robustness and calibration are separate properties, and the swap only guarantees the first.

scenes.title: Distance and Density — kNN, LOF, Mahalanobis
scenes.description: From "far from the centre" to "far from its own neighbours" — kNN distance, LOF, Mahalanobis, and the dimension at which all of them stop working.
scenes.markdown:
# Distance and density

Scene 2 asked *how far is this value from the middle*. That question has no answer once the data has structure — several clusters, different densities, correlated axes. This scene replaces it three times.

## kNN distance

$$\mathrm{score}(a) = d\bigl(a,\, a^{(k)}\bigr)$$

where $a^{(k)}$ is the $k$-th nearest neighbour. Simple, assumption-free, and still one of the strongest baselines in the benchmark literature. Its failure is that the threshold is **global** while density is **local**.

## Local Outlier Factor

Breunig et al., 2000. Three definitions stacked:

$$\text{reach-dist}_k(a, b) = \max\bigl(k\text{-distance}(b),\; d(a, b)\bigr)$$
$$\mathrm{lrd}_k(a) = \left(\frac{1}{k}\sum_{b \in N_k(a)} \text{reach-dist}_k(a, b)\right)^{-1}$$
$$\mathrm{LOF}_k(a) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{b \in N_k(a)} \frac{\mathrm{lrd}_k(b)}{\mathrm{lrd}_k(a)}$$

The last line is the whole idea: a **ratio** of your neighbourhood's density to your own. $\mathrm{LOF} \approx 1$ means *as crowded as the company I keep*. The score is dimensionless and comparable between regions of different density, which is exactly what kNN distance is not.

Neighbours: **COF** for correlation-shaped neighbourhoods, **INFLO** for clusters of unequal density touching each other, and **DBSCAN**'s noise points, which are a free by-product of clustering rather than a score.

## Mahalanobis distance

$$d_M(a) = \sqrt{(a - \mu)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(a - \mu)}$$

Euclidean distance measured in the shape of the data: whiten by the covariance, then measure. Its own contamination problem is severe, because $\Sigma$ is estimated from the same data — the standard fix is the **Minimum Covariance Determinant** estimator, which is what scikit-learn's `EllipticEnvelope` uses.

## The dimension where this all stops

Relative contrast $(d_{\max} - d_{\min})/d_{\min}$ on uniform points, measured on screen:

| $d$ | 2 | 3 | 5 | 10 | 20 | 40 | 64 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| contrast | 29.1 | 9.3 | 4.2 | 1.8 | 0.96 | 0.61 | 0.44 |

Past about $d = 20$ the farthest point is less than twice as far as the nearest. "Far from its neighbours" has stopped meaning anything. The escapes are **subspace methods**, **feature bagging**, **random projections**, and — the one that actually won — **learned representations**, which is scene 5.
scenes.prompt: Scene 3 of six. The dataset is deliberately constructed so that the global and local answers DISAGREE: a tight cluster of 90 points at (-2.2, 0) with sd 0.25, a loose cluster of 60 at (2.4, 0) with sd 1.0, and three planted strays. At k = 20 the tight cluster's kNN distances have median 0.27, the loose cluster's median 1.30, and the strays sit at 1.22, 2.97 and 1.84 -- so the quietest stray is BELOW the loose cluster's median and no global kNN threshold can catch all three strays without flagging half the loose cluster. LOF fixes it: tight median 1.10, loose median 1.04, strays 3.46, 3.52, 5.19, so a threshold of 2 catches all three and nothing else. Those numbers are computed live, not quoted. The second half is Mahalanobis on a correlated cloud where the Euclidean and Mahalanobis orderings of two planted points are REVERSED: the point along the ridge is Euclidean 4.58 but Mahalanobis 2.28, the point across it is Euclidean 1.98 but Mahalanobis 3.98. The scene closes by measuring distance concentration, so the curse of dimensionality is a plotted curve rather than a claim. Do not oversell LOF -- it has its own failure modes (k below about 10 is noisy, k above the smallest real cluster stops being local, and it degrades in high dimension exactly like kNN).

steps.title: One cloud, two densities
steps.description:
153 points. A **tight** cluster on the left (90 points, $\sigma = 0.25$), a **loose** one on the right (60 points, $\sigma = 1.0$), and three strays that belong to neither.

Both clusters are *normal*. The difference between them is not anomaly, it is **scale** — and scale is exactly what a single global distance threshold cannot accommodate.

Nothing is flagged yet. Look at the three strays and ask yourself what distance would separate them from the loose cluster.
steps.prompt: Set-up only. No detector has run. Push the student to make the prediction: what single distance would separate the three strays from the loose cluster? The answer is none, and the next step proves it with the actual numbers. Both clusters are legitimately normal -- the loose one is not anomalous, it is just less dense, and conflating low density with anomaly is precisely the error the scene is about to expose.

add.label: 153 points, two densities
add.prompt: The dataset. Indices 0-89 are the tight cluster, 90-149 the loose one, 150-152 the three planted strays at (-2.2, 1.35), (-0.2, 2.6) and (-3.6, -1.5). Note that two of the three strays sit near the TIGHT cluster -- they are anomalous because of where they are relative to their own neighbourhood, not because they are far from the global centre.

steps.title: kNN distance — the k-th neighbour, and the threshold that fails
steps.description:
Score every point by its distance to its $k$-th nearest neighbour, then flag everything above $\tau$. Drag $\tau$.

The right-hand plot is the score itself: one bar-height per point, index on the $x$-axis, with the three planted strays marked in red and your threshold as a gold line.

At $k = 20$: the tight cluster's scores have median $0.27$, the loose cluster's median $1.30$, and the three strays sit at $1.22$, $2.97$ and $1.84$. **The quietest stray scores lower than a typical loose-cluster point.**

So there is no $\tau$ that works. Lower it until it catches the stray at $1.22$ and you have flagged half the loose cluster with it. Raise it until the loose cluster is clean and two of the three strays escape. Try — the count is in the panel.
steps.prompt: The failure, and the student should verify it by dragging tau rather than taking it on faith. The exact numbers at k = 20: tight cluster kNN median 0.27 with 95th percentile 0.53, loose cluster median 1.30, strays 1.22, 2.97, 1.84. Since 1.22 < 1.30, catching the quietest stray requires a threshold below the loose cluster's median. The diagnosis matters more than the failure: the score is an ABSOLUTE distance, but what makes a point anomalous is how its distance compares to its NEIGHBOURS' distances. Every fix in this scene is a way of making the score relative.

steps.title: Make the score relative: LOF
steps.description:
Same neighbourhoods, one change: instead of reporting your distance, report **the ratio of your neighbours' density to your own**.

$$\mathrm{LOF}_k(a) = \frac{1}{k}\sum_{b \in N_k(a)} \frac{\mathrm{lrd}_k(b)}{\mathrm{lrd}_k(a)}$$

A point in the loose cluster has low density — but so do all its neighbours, so the ratio is about $1$. A stray has low density while its *neighbours* do not, so the ratio is large. The units cancel. The score is comparable across regions that are not comparable in distance.

At $k = 20$: tight cluster median $1.10$, loose cluster median $1.04$, strays $3.46$, $3.52$, $5.19$. **A threshold of $2$ catches all three and nothing else** — and the gap is wide enough that the exact value hardly matters.

That is the difference between a score you have to tune and a score you can reason about.
steps.prompt: The fix. Make sure the student sees WHY the ratio works -- the denominator is the point's own density and the numerator is its neighbourhood's, so a uniformly sparse region cancels to 1 while a sparse point in a dense region does not. The scale-free property is the prize: LOF is dimensionless and comparable between regions, kNN distance is neither. Honest limits, which the step text does not have room for: below about k = 10 LOF is noisy because lrd is estimated from too few neighbours; above the size of the smallest genuine cluster it stops being local and that cluster starts scoring as anomalous wholesale; and in high dimension it degrades exactly like kNN, for the reason the last step measures. Let the student drag k to the extremes and watch both failures happen.

If the student drags k below about 8, watch the band widen and false positives appear; above about 40 the tight cluster's own structure starts to matter.

steps.title: Mahalanobis — distance in the shape of the data
steps.description:
A different failure of Euclidean distance, and a different fix.

This cloud is strongly correlated: $\sigma = 2.2$ along the ridge, $0.35$ across it. Two points are marked.

- The **blue** point is far out along the ridge. Euclidean distance from the mean: $4.58$.
- The **red** point is close to the mean. Euclidean distance: $1.98$.

By Euclidean distance the blue point is the outlier, by more than a factor of two. But the blue point is doing exactly what every other point does, just more of it, while the red point is somewhere this data never goes.

$$d_M(a) = \sqrt{(a - \mu)^{\top}\Sigma^{-1}(a - \mu)}$$

Mahalanobis: blue $2.28$, red $3.98$. **The ordering reverses**, and the ellipse on screen is why — it is the locus $d_M = 2$, and you can see which point is outside it.

The catch is the same one as scene 2: $\Sigma$ is estimated from data that contains the outliers, so a few bad points inflate the ellipse until it swallows them. The fix is a robust covariance — **Minimum Covariance Determinant**, the estimator behind `EllipticEnvelope`, which fits $\Sigma$ on the least-scattered half of the data.
steps.prompt: Mahalanobis, and the reversal. The two marked points are indices 160 (along the ridge, Euclidean 4.58, Mahalanobis 2.28) and 161 (across the ridge, Euclidean 1.98, Mahalanobis 3.98). The drawn ellipse is the exact locus of Mahalanobis distance 2, computed from the eigen-decomposition of the sample covariance -- scripts/check_anomaly_domain.py verifies that every drawn vertex has Mahalanobis distance exactly 2. The intuition to offer: Mahalanobis is Euclidean distance after whitening, i.e. after rescaling each principal direction by its own standard deviation, so it measures 'how many sigmas, in the direction that matters'. The contamination caveat is not optional -- the covariance is estimated from the same contaminated data, and MCD exists because of it.

steps.title: Where all of this stops working
steps.description:
Every method in this scene rests on one assumption: that *far* and *near* are meaningfully different. Here is that assumption, measured.

Draw 120 points uniformly in the unit cube of $d$ dimensions. For each point find its nearest and farthest neighbour, and take the **relative contrast**

$$\frac{d_{\max} - d_{\min}}{d_{\min}}.$$

In 2 dimensions it is about $29$: the farthest point is thirty times as far as the nearest, and "far" means something. By $d = 20$ it is $0.96$ — the farthest point is less than twice as far as the nearest. By $d = 64$ it is $0.44$.

Nothing is broken; the geometry simply stops cooperating. Volume concentrates near the surface, every pair of random points ends up at nearly the same distance, and a score built on that distance is ranking noise.

## The four escapes

1. **Subspace methods** — score in many low-dimensional projections and combine. *(HiCS, SOD)*
2. **Feature bagging** — the ensemble version of the same idea.
3. **Random projections** — Johnson–Lindenstrauss says you can keep pairwise distances while cutting dimension; it does not say the *contrast* returns.
4. **Learn a representation in which distance means something again.** This is the one that won, and it is scene 5.

## Carry forward

- A score you have to tune per region is a score that has not solved the problem. Make it **relative** (LOF) or **whiten** it (Mahalanobis).
- Every estimator in this scene — $\Sigma$ especially — is fitted on contaminated data. Ask what its breakdown point is.
- Check your dimensionality before trusting any distance-based detector. Twenty is already a lot.
steps.prompt: The measured curse. The numbers on the curve are real: relative contrast 29.10 at d = 2, 9.26 at d = 3, 4.24 at d = 5, 1.78 at d = 10, 0.96 at d = 20, 0.61 at d = 40, 0.44 at d = 64, each computed from 120 seeded uniform points with exact nearest and farthest neighbours. d = 1 is omitted from the plot because one near-coincident pair sends the statistic into the thousands. Two clarifications worth having ready. First, concentration is about UNIFORM or unstructured data -- real high-dimensional data often lies near a low-dimensional manifold, which is precisely why learned representations help and why the curse is a warning rather than a proof of impossibility. Second, Johnson-Lindenstrauss preserves pairwise distances under random projection but does not restore contrast; it makes computation cheaper, not the problem easier.

Nothing here is theoretical; every value is 120 seeded uniform points with their exact extreme neighbours.

proof.title: Why Mahalanobis reverses Euclidean order — it is Euclidean distance after whitening
proof.techniqueHint: Diagonalise the covariance, change coordinates, and the quadratic form collapses to a plain squared norm. The reversal on screen is then arithmetic, not intuition.
proof.goal: Show that $d_M(x) = \lVert \Lambda^{-1/2} Q^{\top}(x - \mu) \rVert$ — Mahalanobis distance is ordinary Euclidean distance measured after rescaling each principal axis by its own standard deviation — and that its level sets are therefore the ellipses drawn on screen.
proof.prompt: The proof behind scene 3's second half. The scene SHOWS the ordering reversal but never says why it happens; this derives it. The one move that matters is the change of coordinates: once you write Sigma = Q Lambda Q^T and set z = Lambda^{-1/2} Q^T (x - mu), the quadratic form is literally ||z||^2, so Mahalanobis IS Euclidean -- in the coordinate system where the data is round. Everything else follows: the level sets are spheres in z, hence ellipses in x with semi-axes proportional to sqrt(lambda_i), which is exactly the ellipse drawn. If a student asks why Sigma is invertible here, it is symmetric positive definite whenever the data is not confined to a lower-dimensional subspace. The closing caveat is not optional and is the same one as scene 2: Sigma is ESTIMATED from data that contains the outliers, so a few bad points inflate the ellipse until it swallows them -- which is what MCD and EllipticEnvelope exist to fix. Breakdown point is the link back to scene 2.

dm.label: d_M — the distance the ellipse on screen measures

steps.justification: A quadratic form in the centred coordinates, with the inverse covariance as its matrix.
steps.explanation: Setting $\Sigma = I$ recovers squared Euclidean distance exactly. So Mahalanobis is not a different *kind* of distance — it is Euclidean distance with the identity replaced by what the data actually did.

nodes.description: Σ — the covariance, estimated from this very cloud

steps.label: Σ is symmetric positive definite, so it diagonalises
steps.justification: The spectral theorem applies because $\Sigma$ is symmetric: $Q$ is orthogonal and $\Lambda$ is diagonal, $\Lambda = \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1, \ldots, \lambda_d)$. The eigenvalues are strictly positive whenever the data is not confined to a lower-dimensional subspace, since $v^{\top}\Sigma v$ is the sample variance along $v$.
steps.explanation: The columns of $Q$ are the principal directions — on screen, the ridge and the direction across it — and $\lambda_i$ is the variance along each. Positive definiteness is what makes the next line legal.

steps.label: Whiten: rescale each principal axis by its own σ

z.label: z — the coordinates in which this cloud is round

steps.justification: Inverting $\Sigma = Q\Lambda Q^{\top}$ uses $Q^{-1} = Q^{\top}$, so $\Sigma^{-1} = Q\Lambda^{-1}Q^{\top}$. Each $\lambda_i^{-1/2}$ exists by positive definiteness.
steps.explanation: Two operations, in order: $Q^{\top}$ rotates the ridge onto a coordinate axis, then $\Lambda^{-1/2}$ divides each axis by its own standard deviation. The cloud comes out spherical with unit variance in every direction.

nodes.description: z — the coordinates in which this cloud is round

steps.label: In those coordinates the quadratic form is just a squared norm
steps.justification: Split $\Lambda^{-1} = \Lambda^{-1/2}\Lambda^{-1/2}$ and regroup, using that $\Lambda^{-1/2}$ is diagonal hence symmetric.
steps.explanation: This is the whole proof in one line. **Mahalanobis distance is Euclidean distance** — just measured in the coordinate system where the data has no preferred direction and no preferred scale. Nothing exotic is happening; the exotic part was the coordinate system you started in.

steps.label: So the level sets are the ellipses on screen
steps.justification: The whitening map is a bijection, so the preimage of the sphere $\lVert z \rVert = c$ is its image under the inverse map $x = \mu + Q\Lambda^{1/2} z$.
steps.explanation: A sphere pushed through $Q\Lambda^{1/2}$ is an ellipsoid whose semi-axis along the $i$-th principal direction has length $c\sqrt{\lambda_i}$. The curve drawn in the scene is this set at $c = 2$ — not a sketch of one, but the exact locus.

steps.label: Which is why the ordering reverses
steps.math: \lVert x - \mu \rVert \;\text{large},\; \htmlClass{hl-dm}{d_M(x)} \;\text{small} \iff x-\mu \;\text{lies along a direction with large}\; \lambda_i
steps.justification: Euclidean distance weights every direction by $1$; Mahalanobis weights direction $i$ by $\lambda_i^{-1/2}$. The two orderings therefore disagree exactly when the competing displacements lie along axes of very different variance.
steps.explanation:
On screen: the blue point is Euclidean $4.58$ but Mahalanobis $2.28$, the red point Euclidean $1.98$ but Mahalanobis $3.98$. The blue point is far along the *wide* axis, doing what every point does but more so; the red point is a short way along the *narrow* one, somewhere this data never goes.

The caveat is scene 2's, returning in matrix form: $\Sigma$ is **estimated from the contaminated sample**. A few outliers inflate the very eigenvalues that are supposed to expose them, and the ellipse grows until it swallows them — masking again, with breakdown point $0$. That is what the Minimum Covariance Determinant estimator behind `EllipticEnvelope` exists to fix: it fits $\Sigma$ on the least-scattered half of the data, buying back a breakdown point near $1/2$.

scenes.title: Isolation Forest and One-Class Boundaries
scenes.description: Two ideas that stop modelling normal and start modelling separability — the Isolation Forest's path length, and the level set a one-class boundary actually is.
scenes.markdown:
# Isolation and one-class boundaries

Every method so far built a model of *normal* and measured departures from it. Two families refuse to.

## Isolation Forest — Liu, Ting & Zhou, 2008

Don't profile normal points. Ask instead: **how few random cuts does it take to separate this point from everything else?**

Build a tree by repeatedly picking a random feature and a uniformly random split inside its observed range. Anomalies sit in sparse regions, so a random cut is more likely to land on the empty side of them, and they fall out of the tree early. Let $h(x)$ be the depth at which $x$ becomes a leaf, averaged over a forest:

$$s(x) = 2^{-\,\mathbb{E}[h(x)]\,/\,c(\psi)}, \qquad c(n) = 2H(n-1) - \frac{2(n-1)}{n}$$

$c(\psi)$ is the expected path length of an unsuccessful search in a binary search tree of $\psi$ nodes — the normalisation that makes scores comparable across sample sizes. $s \to 1$ means isolated in very few cuts; $s \approx 0.5$ means an ordinary point.

Three properties worth knowing:
- **Linear time, constant memory**, and no distance computation at all — which is why it survives dimensions where scene 3's methods do not.
- **Subsampling helps.** The canonical $\psi = 256$ is not a compromise for speed; small samples *reduce* swamping and masking, because a subsample is less likely to contain the dense cluster that hides an anomaly.
- **The splits are axis-parallel**, which leaves visible rectangular artefacts in the score field. **Extended Isolation Forest** cuts with random hyperplanes instead and removes them.

## One-class boundaries

The other refusal: draw a region containing (most of) the data and call the outside anomalous.

- **One-Class SVM** (Schölkopf) — maximum-margin separation from the origin in feature space. $\nu$ upper-bounds the fraction of training points rejected and lower-bounds the fraction of support vectors; $\gamma$ sets the RBF kernel width.
- **SVDD** (Tax & Duin) — the smallest enclosing hypersphere, equivalent to the above for the RBF kernel.
- **Elliptic Envelope** — the parametric version: one Gaussian, robustly fitted, and scene 3's ellipse is the boundary.

> **What is actually drawn here.** The boundary on screen is the $\nu$-quantile level set of the Gaussian kernel density $\frac1n\sum_j e^{-\gamma\lVert x - x_j\rVert^2}$ — the **full-rank** version of the object a One-Class SVM approximates with a sparse set of support vectors. It is not a One-Class SVM, and the difference is real: the SVM's sparsity is what makes it tractable and is half of why it is used. What carries over is $\gamma$, the kernel width, exactly; and $\nu$ only as an **operational analogue**. Here $\nu$ is a lower-tail cutoff on the training points' own densities — an interpolated empirical quantile — so it rejects *approximately* $\nu$ of them ($\nu = 0.1$ rejects $0.101$ of this training set). The SVM's $\nu$ is a bound, not a rate: it upper-bounds the rejected fraction and lower-bounds the support-vector fraction. Same knob, same direction, different guarantee.

### The kernel is the prior

**We picked this kernel by hand.** Nothing chose it for us and nothing in the data
suggested it — $k_\gamma(x, x') = e^{-\gamma\lVert x - x'\rVert^2}$, the Gaussian RBF,
is an assumption we brought with us. It is worth being blunt about, because it is
doing more of the work here than either slider.

A kernel is an answer to *"which points count as near each other"*, decided **before
you look**. That is an **inductive bias**, and the RBF's is specific:

- **Isotropy** — the same in every direction. *Fails when* the data is elongated or correlated.
- **Stationarity** — one $\gamma$ everywhere. *Fails when* clusters have different densities.
- **Smooth decay** — far points contribute nothing. *Fails when* the structure is long-range.

Watch what that costs. Sweeping $\gamma$ across two orders of magnitude, the best this
density ever does:

- on the **ring** — radially symmetric data, radially symmetric kernel — **8 of 8**;
- on **dense**, the two-cluster set from scene 3 — **2 of 3**, and no $\gamma$ in a 61-point sweep from $10^{-2}$ to $10^{2}$ does better.

The ring was built as a ring and the RBF is radial, so its bias is correct **by
construction**. That is why the demonstration is so clean, and it is the part a
demonstration never shows you. On `dense` the same kernel cannot win at any setting,
because one bandwidth everywhere is exactly the assumption LOF was invented to escape.

So $\gamma$ is not a tuning knob so much as a **strength dial on the prior**: small
$\gamma$ asserts strong smoothness and underfits, large $\gamma$ asserts almost none and
memorises the training points. The next step lets you drag it and watch both failures.

This is the honest reading of *no free lunch*: every unsupervised detector is a
different bias, and which one wins is a question about your data, not about the method.

## Ensembles

No single detector wins, so average several. The one rule: **you can only average scores that are on a comparable scale.** An Isolation Forest score lives in $(0,1)$, a kNN distance in the units of your features, a LOF around $1$. Standardise, or convert to ranks, before you combine — otherwise the loudest scale wins the vote. *(Feature bagging; LSCP for locally selective combination.)*
scenes.prompt: Scene 4 of six. Two families that model separability rather than normality. The Isolation Forest is real: 100 trees, subsample 128 without replacement, uniformly random axis and uniformly random split inside the observed range, depth capped at ceil(log2 psi), leaves crediting c(size) for the subtree not built -- Liu's estimator exactly, and the checker verifies that adIsoGrid equals 2^(-adIsoDepth/c(128)) to machine precision. c(128) = 8.866294. One honest caveat if a student pushes on the proof: the random-BST step is a MODEL, not a consequence of the split rule. A uniform split VALUE makes a rank's probability proportional to its gap width, not uniform; measured at n=8, uniform data gives 1/(n-1), Gaussian data is U-shaped (~0.19 at the edges vs ~0.11 in the middle), and with one far outlier the root split isolates it alone 93% of the time. That last fact is the mechanism, not a bug. c(n) is Liu's normaliser borrowed from BST theory. The heatmap shows the score over the plane and the axis-parallel artefacts in it are REAL, not a rendering defect: they are the reason Extended Isolation Forest exists. The one-class half needs an honesty caveat that must not be skipped -- the drawn boundary is the nu-quantile level set of a Gaussian kernel density, the full-rank object a One-Class SVM approximates with sparse support vectors. It is not an SVM. nu and gamma are OPERATIONAL ANALOGUES, not the SVM's guarantees: here nu is a lower-tail cutoff on the training densities, an interpolated empirical quantile, so it rejects approximately nu -- nu = 0.1 rejects 0.101 of this training set. In a nu-SVM, nu is an upper bound on the training-error fraction and a lower bound on the support-vector fraction. Gamma is the kernel width in both. The ring dataset is non-convex on purpose: four planted points sit in the hole, where no ellipse can exclude them but a level set can, and the boundary has two walls. steps.title: Isolation Forest: stop modelling normal, count cuts
steps.description:
Pick a feature at random. Pick a split point uniformly inside its observed range. Recurse. Stop when a point is alone.

A point in a dense region needs many cuts before the region around it is empty. A point out on its own gets separated almost immediately, because almost any cut has it on one side by itself.

So **the depth at which a point falls out of the tree is itself an anomaly score** — no distance, no density estimate, no covariance, no model of what normal looks like. Average that depth over a forest of 100 trees, each built on a subsample of 128 points, and you have the Isolation Forest.

The chart is the resulting score for all 192 points of the scene-1 cloud. Red are the planted twelve.

Practical consequences worth naming: linear time, constant memory, no distance computation, and therefore no dependence on the distance concentration that ended scene 3. The scores here run about 0.53 for a typical inlier against 0.72 and above for the planted points. If a student asks why the inliers are near 0.5 rather than 0: 0.5 is where a point of exactly average path length lands, by construction of the 2^(-E[h]/c) score, so 0.5 means ordinary and 1 means trivially isolated.

steps.description:
A different refusal to model normal: pick a region that contains most of the data, and flag whatever falls outside.

This cloud is an annulus with four points planted in the hole and four outside. It is **non-convex**, and that matters: no ellipse, no half-space, nothing convex can exclude the hole. Scene 3's Mahalanobis ellipse would put its centre right in the middle of the emptiest region and call those four points the most normal in the dataset.

The purple curves are the **$\nu$-quantile level set** of the Gaussian kernel density. Two of them, because the region has two walls.

**$\nu$** is not a tuning knob you have to search — it is the fraction of the training data you are choosing to reject. Set $\nu = 0.1$ and about $10\%$ of the training points land outside — $10.1\%$ here, because the cutoff is an interpolated empirical quantile and the membership test keeps ties. That is what makes it usable: you specify your alert budget directly.

steps.description:
Now drag **$\gamma$**.

**Small $\gamma$** — wide kernels. Every point's influence reaches far, the density is smooth, and the boundary becomes a blob that ignores the hole entirely. Underfitting: the model of normal is too generous and the four points in the middle go undetected.

**Large $\gamma$** — narrow kernels. Each point only supports density in its immediate vicinity, and the boundary collapses onto the training points themselves, shrink-wrapping individual observations and the gaps between them.

*How the curve is drawn:* each of the 128 rays keeps its first crossing outward and its last crossing inward, so what you see is the **outer and inner wall of a single annulus**. Once large $\gamma$ genuinely fragments the level set into islands, the rays have more crossings than the two that are kept and the drawn curve stops being the level set. Read the large-$\gamma$ picture as *the boundary is breaking up*, not as a faithful outline of the pieces.

That second failure is worth sitting with. At large $\gamma$ the detector has near-perfect *training* behaviour — every training point is inside, everything else is out — and has learned nothing. A **new** normal observation, landing a little away from any training point, is flagged.

This is ordinary overfitting, in a setting where you usually have no labelled validation set to catch it with. Which is the real difficulty of one-class methods: **the model-selection problem has no clean answer when you cannot measure generalisation.** In practice: hold out clean data if you have any, watch the flag *rate* rather than the flag *set*, and prefer the smoother model when in doubt.

Be straight about the rendering if asked: the tracer keeps one crossing pair per ray, so it draws a single annulus and CANNOT outline disconnected islands; past the point of fragmentation the drawn curve is indicative, not the true level set. The deep point is the one about model selection: at large gamma training behaviour is near-perfect and generalisation is destroyed, and unlike supervised learning there is usually no labelled validation set to reveal it. Concrete advice if asked: hold out clean data when you have it, monitor the FLAG RATE over time rather than the flag set, prefer the smoother model, and note that scikit-learn's 'scale' heuristic sets gamma from the feature variance for exactly this reason. steps.title: Combining detectors, and the rule that makes it legal
steps.description:
You now have five scores for the same point: an isolation score, a LOF, a kNN distance, a kernel density and a Mahalanobis distance. (The modified z-score from scene 2 is a 1-D statistic and has no reading on this two-dimensional cloud, which is itself the point — not every detector even applies to every problem.) They disagree, and no benchmark says which to trust in general.

So average them. One rule makes that legal:

> **You can only average scores that are on a comparable scale.**

Look at what these actually produce: isolation in $(0,1)$ with ordinary at $0.5$; LOF around $1$ and unbounded above; kNN distance in whatever units your features have; kernel density in units of $1/\text{area}$. Average them raw and the one with the largest numerical spread decides every vote, for no reason connected to the data.

**Two honest normalisations.**
1. **Standardise** each score — subtract its mean, divide by its sd — then average. Cheap, but it assumes the scores are roughly symmetric, and anomaly scores are by construction skewed.
2. **Convert to ranks** and average those. Throws away magnitude, keeps ordering, and is immune to any monotone rescaling. Usually the right default.

**Other combinations worth knowing.** *Maximum* of standardised scores (catch anything any detector dislikes — high recall, low precision). *Average of maximum* over random feature subsets, which is **feature bagging**. **LSCP**, which picks which detectors to trust *per point* using local performance.

## Carry forward

- Isolation Forest is the strongest cheap default on tabular data: no distances, linear time, handles high dimension, few knobs. Start there.
- If you need a *region* rather than a score — a rule to ship, a boundary to draw — a one-class method gives you one, and $\nu$ lets you state your alert budget directly.
- Every method here is still fitted on contaminated data. $\nu$ at least makes the assumption explicit: you are *declaring* the contamination rate rather than hoping it is small.
- Ensemble by ranks, not by raw scores.
steps.prompt: Closing step. The single rule -- only average comparable scales -- is the most portable thing in the scene, and the failure it prevents is concrete: raw-averaging a kNN distance in feature units with an isolation score in (0,1) lets the distance decide every vote. Rank averaging is the recommended default because it is invariant to any monotone rescaling and anomaly scores are badly skewed. Name the variants if asked: maximum of standardised scores for recall, feature bagging (average of maximum over random feature subsets) for high dimension, LSCP for per-point detector selection. The forward hinge is that all five detectors output a SCORE and none of them outputs a decision, which is what scene 6 is about -- though scene 5 comes first and asks whether a learned representation can beat all of them.

proof.title: Why the Isolation Forest score is 2^(−E[h]/c(n))
proof.techniqueHint: An isolation tree built by random splits is MODELLED by a random binary search tree, whose expected path length is already known. The model is an idealisation — it is exact for rank-uniform splitting, while the estimator splits on a uniform value — so c(n) is borrowed as the normaliser rather than derived from the estimator.
proof.goal: Derive $c(n) = 2H_{n-1} - \dfrac{2(n-1)}{n}$ as the expected external path length of a random binary search tree on $n$ keys, and show why dividing by it makes $s(x) = 2^{-\mathbb{E}[h(x)]/c(n)}$ comparable across sample sizes.
proof.prompt: The normalisation nobody explains. The key move in step two is a MODELLING ASSUMPTION, and must be presented as one: the random-BST model is exact for rank-uniform splitting, while this estimator splits on a uniform VALUE, which makes a rank's probability proportional to its gap width. Measured at n=8: uniform data gives 1/(n-1), Gaussian data is U-shaped (~0.19 edges vs ~0.11 middle), and with one far outlier the root split isolates it alone 93% of the time -- which is the mechanism the method runs on, not a defect. So c(n) is the normaliser Liu BORROWS from the solved BST problem, not a quantity derived from this estimator. From there c(n) = 2H(n-1) - 2(n-1)/n. The ln n + gamma asymptotic is the usual shorthand, but the library sums H exactly: the asymptotic is 27.6% low at n=3 and 14.5% low at n=4, and depth-capped trees hit small leaves constantly. The last step is the one that makes it a SCORE: because E[h] grows like log n, dividing by c(n) makes the exponent a ratio around 1 that no longer depends on the subsample size, and 2^(-1) = 0.5 is therefore where an average point lands by construction. If a student asks why base 2, it is the natural base for a binary tree and any other base would just rescale the exponent.

steps.label: An isolation tree splits uniformly at random

split.label: the split point — uniform in the observed range

steps.justification: The construction of Liu, Ting & Zhou (2008). No label, no target, no distance is consulted at any point.
steps.explanation: The split is uniform over the *observed range of that node's data*, not over a fixed global range. That is what lets the tree adapt to the region it is currently in.

steps.label: Its depth profile is that of a random BST
steps.math: \text{random-BST model:}\quad \Pr[\text{left subtree has } i \text{ of } n-1] = \frac{1}{n}, \quad 0 \le i \le n-1
steps.justification: Exact when the *rank* of the splitting element is uniform — splitting on a randomly chosen key. The tree here splits on a uniformly chosen **value** in $[\min, \max]$, so a rank's probability is proportional to its gap width instead. Measured at the root with $n = 8$: uniform data gives $1/(n-1)$ on $i = 1 \ldots n-1$ (never $0$, since an empty side is made a leaf); Gaussian data is U-shaped, about $0.19$ at the edges against $0.11$ in the middle; and with one far outlier the split isolates it alone $93\%$ of the time. That last number is not a defect — gap-proportional splitting isolating outliers fast is precisely *why the method works*. So $c(n)$ below is the **standard normaliser borrowed from BST theory**, which is how Liu uses it, not a quantity derived from this estimator.
steps.explanation: This is the step that does all the work — and it is a **modelling assumption**, not a consequence of the split rule above it. It buys the answer from a very old problem: the average path length of a binary search tree built from a uniformly random permutation.

nodes.subexpr: \text{random-BST model:}\quad \Pr[\text{left subtree has } i \text{ of } n-1] = \frac{1}{n}
\text{random-BST model:} \Pr \left(\text{left subtree has } i \text{ of } n - 1\right)

steps.label: The external path length satisfies a standard recurrence
steps.justification: Averaging the depth of an unsuccessful search over both subtrees, weighted by the uniform subtree-size distribution, and adding one edge for the current node on each of the $n-1$ non-root insertions.
steps.explanation: The $2(n-1)/n$ term is the cost of descending past the root; the sum is the recursive cost below it, and the $1/n$ is the split probability from the step above. Check it against the closed form: $c(3) = \tfrac13 c(1) + \tfrac13 c(2) + \tfrac43 = \tfrac53$, which is $2H_2 - \tfrac43$.

steps.label: Solve it with harmonic numbers
steps.justification: Standard: multiply the recurrence by $n$, subtract the same relation at $n-1$ to remove the sum, and telescope.
steps.explanation: So $c(128) = 8.8663$ and $c(256) = 10.2487$. The growth is logarithmic, which is the fact the next step depends on.

steps.label: Normalise, then exponentiate

h.label: h(x) — the depth at which x is isolated

c.label: c(ψ) — the expected depth for this subsample size

steps.justification: The exponent is a ratio of two path lengths, so the subsample size cancels; the exponential maps $[0, \infty)$ onto $(0, 1]$ with the average case at $\tfrac12$.
steps.explanation: That is the whole design. Without $c(\psi)$ the raw depth would grow like $\log \psi$ and a forest on 128 points would produce systematically smaller numbers than one on 256, for no reason connected to the data. With it, $0.5$ means *ordinary* and $1$ means *isolated immediately*, at any $\psi$.

scenes.description: Reconstruction error as an anomaly score, the capacity trap that kills it, and an honest tour of what deep learning and foundation models did and did not solve.
scenes.markdown:
# Learned representations

Every method so far used the coordinates you were given. This scene learns new ones.

## Reconstruction as a score

Train a model to compress and rebuild its input through a bottleneck. It can only learn to rebuild what it has seen often. So

$$\mathrm{score}(x) = \lVert x - \mathrm{decode}(\mathrm{encode}(x)) \rVert$$

is an anomaly score. This is the **autoencoder** detector, and everything below is a variation on it.

The model on screen is a *linear* autoencoder — keep the $r$ lowest Fourier modes, discard the rest. Small enough to reason about, and it has every pathology the deep version has.

## The zoo, and what each one is actually for

| Family | Idea | Its characteristic failure |
|---|---|---|
| **Autoencoder** | Reconstruct through a bottleneck | Generalises too well and reconstructs the anomaly |
| **Denoising AE** | Reconstruct a corrupted input | Better, and the corruption is another hyperparameter |
| **VAE** | Probabilistic; score by likelihood | Likelihood is famously *not* a good OOD score |
| **DeepSVDD** | Learn an embedding, minimise a hypersphere | Hypersphere collapse — a constant encoder scores perfectly |
| **DeepSAD** | DeepSVDD plus a few labels | Needs those labels |
| **AnoGAN / GANomaly** | Score by how hard the point is to generate | Unstable training; largely superseded |
| **Self-supervised** | Pretext task; score by how badly it is solved | The pretext task is the whole design |
| **Embedding + kNN** | Pretrained encoder, then scene 3 | Brutally effective, and rarely the paper |

## Sequences

For time series the reconstruction idea becomes **forecast residual**: predict the next point from the past, score by the error. ARIMA → LSTM → Transformer is the same idea at three capacities. Alongside: **STL** decomposition (score the remainder), **Spectral Residual** (from the saliency literature), and the **matrix profile** (compare every subsequence to every other, no training at all).

**Time-series foundation models** are where the field moved in 2025–26 — pretrained sequence models, adapted for detection (state-aware adapters, foundation autoencoders). They are a genuine improvement on training a model per series.

**General-purpose LLMs as the detector are not.** The surveys are consistent: gains are limited, and putting an LLM at the centre of a detection pipeline is usually unjustified. Where they *do* earn their place is downstream — explaining a flagged window, correlating it with deploys and tickets, drafting the incident note, asking the analyst a clarifying question. Detection is numeric; triage is linguistic. Use each for what it is.

### What the matrix is measuring

Every cell is **AUC-ROC**, and it has a reading that needs no curve: it is the
probability that a random planted anomaly is ranked **above** a random normal point.
That is the Mann-Whitney form, and it is literally what `adDetAuc` computes —

$$\mathrm{AUC} \;=\; \frac{1}{|P|\,|N|}\sum_{a \in P}\ \sum_{b \in N}
\Big(\mathbb{1}[s_a > s_b] + \tfrac12\,\mathbb{1}[s_a = s_b]\Big)$$

with $P$ the planted points, $N$ the rest, and ties counting a half. So **1.0** means
every anomaly outranks every normal point, and **0.5** means the ranking carries no
information at all — a coin flip, which is why the colour scale starts there rather
than at zero.

Two things it deliberately does *not* tell you, both of which scene 6 takes apart:
it is **threshold-free**, so it says nothing about where to cut; and it is
**insensitive to the base rate**, which is exactly why it stays flattering on problems
where precision has already collapsed.

## The result that should shape your priors

Across 30 algorithms and 57 datasets: **no unsupervised method wins everywhere**, and modest supervision beats elaborate architecture. A strong pretrained embedding with a kNN distance on top is a very hard baseline to beat, and it is not in most papers because it is not novel.
scenes.prompt: Scene 5 of six, and the one where the lesson has to be most careful not to oversell. The model is a LINEAR autoencoder -- keep the r lowest Fourier modes of a 128-sample signal -- chosen because it has every pathology the deep version has while remaining fully inspectable. The capacity argument is the scene's spine and the numbers are real: rmseAnom/rmse is 0.75 at r=1 (the anomaly window is LESS wrong than the rest of the signal, so the detector is inverted and would flag the normal parts), 1.98 at r=3 (peak contrast, the sweet spot), and 0.95 by r=10 (the model reconstructs the anomaly as well as the signal and the detector is dead). The signal carries Fourier modes 2 and 3, which is why r=3 is exactly enough. On the AI tour: be accurate about each failure mode, especially that VAE likelihood is a poor OOD score and that DeepSVDD can collapse to a constant encoder. On LLMs be direct -- the 2025-26 survey consensus is that general-purpose LLMs underperform as primary time-series detectors and that time-series FOUNDATION models are the real advance; LLMs earn their place in triage and explanation, not in scoring. Close on ADBench: 30 algorithms, 57 datasets, no universal winner, and embedding-plus-kNN is a very strong baseline.

The grey line is scene 1's signal — the one with a collective anomaly no z-score could see.

The purple line is a model's attempt to rebuild it through a bottleneck of **$r$ components**. This particular model keeps the $r$ lowest Fourier modes and throws the rest away: a *linear* autoencoder, small enough that you can see exactly what it can and cannot represent.

Drag $r$ from 1. At $r = 1$ the model has one mode and the reconstruction is hopeless everywhere. At $r = 3$ it has caught both modes the signal actually contains and tracks it closely — **except across the planted window**, which is not made of those modes.

That gap is the score.
steps.prompt: Introduce reconstruction as a score. The signal genuinely contains Fourier modes 2 and 3 plus noise, so r = 3 is exactly the right capacity and the student can see the reconstruction snap into place there. Emphasise WHY the anomaly survives: the flattened window is not expressible in two low modes, so the model -- which has only learned the normal shape -- cannot reproduce it, and the residual spikes. That is the entire autoencoder-detector idea, with nothing deep about it. If asked what the deep version adds: nonlinearity, so the 'normal manifold' can be curved rather than a linear subspace, and that is the only structural difference.

steps.title: The capacity trap — when the autoencoder rebuilds the anomaly too
steps.description:
Two curves against $r$. **Purple** is the reconstruction error over the whole signal. **Red** is the error restricted to the planted window. The detector only works when red is meaningfully above purple.

Drag $r$ across the range and watch the gap.

| $r$ | overall | window | ratio | verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 2.21 | 1.66 | **0.75** | *inverted* — the window fits **better** than the signal |
| 3 | 0.36 | 0.72 | **1.98** | the sweet spot |
| 10 | 0.29 | 0.28 | **0.95** | dead — the model rebuilds the anomaly too |
| 32 | 0.22 | 0.25 | 1.13 | still dead |

Read that first row again. At $r = 1$ the model is so weak it fits the *flat* stretch better than the oscillating signal around it, so the residual is **lowest** exactly where the anomaly is. The detector does not merely fail; it is **anti-correlated with the truth**, and it would confidently flag the healthy parts.

And the right-hand column is the trap: **overall reconstruction error falls monotonically with capacity, and detection performance does not.** Tuning an autoencoder detector by validation loss — the obvious thing, the thing you would do for any other model — optimises for the wrong quantity and walks you straight to $r = 10$.

This is not an artefact of a linear toy. It is the central practical problem with deep reconstruction detectors, and the mitigations are all attempts to stop the model reconstructing what it has not seen: keep the bottleneck tight, corrupt the input (denoising), train on data you believe is clean, or use a memory-augmented model that can only rebuild from stored normal prototypes.
steps.prompt: The most important step in the scene, and the student must drag through it. The r = 1 row is the one that surprises people: the model is so under-capacitied that it fits the FLAT window better than the oscillating signal, so the residual is smallest exactly where the anomaly is and the detector is anti-correlated with truth. The r = 10 row is the one that costs people money: overall RMSE has fallen to 0.29 and keeps falling, so every ordinary model-selection criterion says 'better', while the contrast ratio has collapsed to 0.95 and the detector is dead. Tuning by validation reconstruction loss is therefore actively wrong for a detector, and that is the transferable lesson. Mitigations, in rough order of usefulness: keep the bottleneck tight and justify its size, train on data you believe is clean (the one-class framing from scene 1), denoising autoencoders, and memory-augmented autoencoders that can only decode from stored normal prototypes. If asked whether this is an artefact of the linear toy: no, it is the central known failure of deep reconstruction detectors and the reason the memory-augmented variants were invented.

steps.title: The zoo — AE, VAE, DeepSVDD, self-supervised, pretrained + kNN
steps.description:
Everything deep in anomaly detection is a variation on *learn normal, score the departure*. The variations differ in **what** they learn and **how** they score, and each has a characteristic way of failing.

**Reconstruction.** Autoencoder (above), denoising AE (reconstruct a corrupted input, so the model cannot copy), **VAE** (probabilistic — but be careful: likelihood is a famously poor out-of-distribution score, and a VAE will happily assign high likelihood to inputs it has never seen).

**Deep one-class.** **DeepSVDD** learns an embedding *and* a minimal enclosing hypersphere at once. Its failure is elegant and fatal: a constant encoder maps everything to the centre and achieves zero radius, so the architecture has to be constrained — no bias terms, no bounded activations — to stop it. **DeepSAD** is the same with a handful of labelled anomalies, and it beats DeepSVDD comfortably, which is scene 1's point again.

**Generative.** AnoGAN and GANomaly score by how hard a point is for a generator to produce. Historically important, unstable to train, largely superseded by reconstruction and self-supervised methods.

**Self-supervised.** Invent a pretext task — predict a rotation, contrast augmented views, reconstruct masked inputs, predict the scale of a random projection — and score by how badly the model solves it on this input. Currently the strongest deep family, and the design work has moved entirely into *choosing the pretext task*.

**Graphs and logs.** GNN-based detection for entities-with-relations; log-template anomaly detection for operational text. Both are the same idea over a different input type.

**The one that quietly wins.** Take a pretrained encoder, embed everything, run scene 3's kNN distance in the embedding space. It is not novel, so it is rarely the paper, and it is frequently the baseline that the paper struggles to beat.
steps.prompt: The tour. Be precise about failure modes -- they are the useful content and the reason to prefer one family over another. VAE: likelihood is not an OOD score, there is a well-known literature of generative models assigning higher likelihood to out-of-distribution inputs than to their own training data. DeepSVDD: hypersphere collapse is real and is why the architecture forbids bias terms and bounded activations; a constant encoder is the trivial optimum. GANs: superseded, say so rather than being diplomatic. Self-supervised: the strongest deep family now, and the design problem has migrated into choosing the pretext task. Embedding plus kNN: emphasise this, it is the recommendation a practitioner should actually leave with. If the student wants a starting point for tabular data, the honest ordering is Isolation Forest first, then embedding + kNN, then a deep method only if those fail and you can measure that they failed.

add.label: AUC-ROC · every detector on every dataset
add.prompt: The no-free-lunch matrix, computed live by adDetAuc rather than pinned: AUC-ROC for each of five detectors on each of three datasets, by the Mann-Whitney identity. axes[0] is rows (detectors, top to bottom: isolation, LOF, kNN, kernel density, Mahalanobis), axes[1] is columns, ordered by WHAT THEY BREAK: 'blob' is one convex Gaussian cloud plus uniform outliers and nothing breaks on it; 'dense' is a tight cluster beside a loose one, which breaks any global radius; 'ring' is an annulus with four points in the hole, which breaks anything convex or centroid-based. The column labels name the shape, not just the tag. Colour is the AUC itself, linearly over [0.5, 1.0] -- 0.5 because that IS chance, so the cold end means a coin flip rather than merely a weak result. Deliberately NOT a contrast-stretched transform: most of these detectors really are near-equal, and exaggerating a 0.012 gap would say they differ when they do not. The one cell that looks different is the one that is. Kernel density is sign-flipped inside adDetAuc since low density is the anomalous case. The readings the three steps draw from it: no row is best everywhere (LOF wins dense and ring but is LAST on blob; isolation wins blob but is 4th on ring); plain kNN is within 0.001 of the best on two of three, which is the 'simple methods are hard to beat' point; and Mahalanobis on ring is 0.500, exactly chance, because the anomalies sit at the mean where an ellipse cannot exclude them.
