steps.title: Sequences and foundation models — and where LLMs actually help
steps.description:
For time series the reconstruction idea becomes **forecast residual**: predict the next value from the past, score by the error. ARIMA, an LSTM and a Transformer are the same idea at three capacities — and they inherit the capacity trap above exactly.

Worth knowing alongside:
- **STL decomposition** — split into trend, season and remainder, score the remainder. Cheap, interpretable, and a strong baseline on anything with a calendar.
- **Spectral Residual** — borrowed from visual saliency; very fast, very few knobs.
- **Matrix profile** — compare every subsequence to every other. No training at all, and it finds collective anomalies like the one in this scene directly.

## Foundation models

**Time-series foundation models** are the real development of 2025–26: pretrained sequence models, adapted for detection with state-aware adapters or used as foundation autoencoders. They remove the per-series training loop, which was most of the operational cost, and they transfer to series you have little history for.

## LLMs

Be careful here, because the marketing and the evidence point in different directions.

The survey consensus is that **general-purpose LLMs underperform as primary time-series detectors**, and that placing one at the centre of a detection pipeline is usually unjustified. Numbers as text is a poor interface to numeric structure, and a detector you cannot calibrate is a detector you cannot operate.

Where they are genuinely good is **everything that happens after the score**:
- explaining *which* features drove a flag, in the vocabulary of the domain;
- correlating a flagged window with deploys, tickets and on-call notes;
- drafting the incident summary;
- asking the analyst the one clarifying question that resolves the ambiguity;
- turning an analyst's "no, that one's fine because…" into a labelled example — which, per scene 1, is worth more than a better model.

**Detection is numeric. Triage is linguistic.** Build the pipeline that way and both halves do what they are good at.
steps.prompt: The sequence and foundation-model step, and the one most likely to be quoted out of context, so be precise. Forecast-residual detectors inherit the capacity trap exactly -- a forecaster good enough to predict the anomaly produces no residual. Name STL, Spectral Residual and the matrix profile as strong non-deep baselines; the matrix profile in particular finds collective anomalies like this scene's directly and needs no training. On foundation models: time-series foundation models are a genuine 2025-26 advance because they remove the per-series training loop and transfer to short-history series; state-aware adapters and foundation autoencoders are the current shape of that work. On LLMs: the survey consensus is that general-purpose LLMs underperform as primary detectors and that centring a pipeline on one is usually unjustified -- say this plainly, do not hedge it. Their real value is post-score: explanation, correlation with deploys and tickets, incident drafting, clarifying questions, and converting an analyst's verbal dismissal into a LABEL, which scene 1 established is worth more than a better model. Detection is numeric, triage is linguistic.

info.title: Detection is numeric
info.content: Every cell is a **number** a detector emitted. An LLM belongs *after* it — never inside the scoring loop.

steps.title: No free lunch — what to actually do
steps.description:
The large tabular benchmark, across 30 algorithms and 57 datasets, reports three things worth building your defaults on.

1. **No unsupervised method wins everywhere.** Any ranking of detectors you read is a ranking on somebody else's data.
2. **A little supervision beats a lot of architecture.** Semi-supervised methods with a handful of labelled anomalies outperform sophisticated unsupervised ones.
3. **Simple methods are hard to beat.** Isolation Forest, kNN distance, and a pretrained embedding with kNN on top are all near the top and all cheap.

## So, an honest default path

1. **Look for labels first.** Thirty examples changes the problem. *(scene 1)*
2. **Plot the thing.** Half of real anomaly detection is a chart nobody made.
3. **Robust statistics** on the obvious univariate signals. *(scene 2)*
4. **Isolation Forest** as the tabular default: fast, few knobs, survives dimension. *(scene 4)*
5. **kNN or LOF** when locality matters and dimension is low. *(scene 3)*
6. **A pretrained embedding + kNN** when the input is text, images or anything with a good encoder.
7. **Train something deep** only when the above have failed *and you can demonstrate that they failed* — which needs scene 6.
8. **An LLM for triage**, never for scoring.

## Which brings us to the question nobody asked yet

Every method in this lesson emits a score. None of them emits a decision. And a score becomes a decision only when someone picks a threshold — at which point the base rate arrives, and everything that looked excellent in this scene may turn out to be unusable.

That is scene 6, and it is the one that decides whether any of this ships.
steps.prompt: The synthesis. Deliver the three ADBench findings as priors rather than trivia: no universal winner, modest supervision beats architecture, simple methods are hard to beat. The eight-step default path is the most practically useful list in the lesson -- walk it with the student if they ask 'so what do I actually do'. Step 2, plot the thing, is not filler: a large share of real anomaly-detection work is a chart nobody made. Step 7 is the load-bearing one: train something deep only when the simple methods have failed AND you can demonstrate that they failed, which requires an evaluation protocol, which is scene 6. Close on the handoff -- every method in the lesson emits a score and none emits a decision, and the base rate is about to make some very good-looking detectors unusable.

scenes.title: Evaluating and Shipping — ROC, PR, and the Base Rate
scenes.description: Where the score becomes a decision: confusion counts, ROC against PR, the base rate that quietly destroys precision, and the operational problems no metric shows you.
scenes.markdown:
# Evaluating and shipping a detector

Five scenes produced scores. None produced a decision. This one is about the cut — and it is where most anomaly-detection projects actually fail.

## Accuracy is not a metric here

At a base rate of $0.1\%$, the model `return NORMAL` scores $99.9\%$ accuracy. Any metric a constant can win is not measuring anything.

## The identity that runs the scene

$$\mathrm{precision} = \frac{\mathrm{TPR}\cdot\pi}{\mathrm{TPR}\cdot\pi + \mathrm{FPR}\cdot(1-\pi)}$$

where $\pi$ is the base rate. It is Bayes' theorem, and it is the same computation as the medical-test problem in the *Conditional Probability* lesson.

Read what it says. **TPR and FPR are properties of the detector. Precision is not.** Precision depends on $\pi$ — on the world, not the model. A detector with $\mathrm{TPR} = 0.8$ and $\mathrm{FPR} = 0.05$ has precision $0.58$ at $\pi = 0.08$ and precision $0.016$ at $\pi = 0.001$. Same detector, same ROC curve, sixty-two of every sixty-three alerts now false.

## ROC-AUC against PR-AUC

ROC plots TPR against FPR. Both are normalised *within* a class, so **ROC-AUC does not depend on the base rate at all** — which is exactly why it is misleading here. It will not move when your problem becomes a hundred times harder.

PR plots precision against recall. Precision has the negative class in its denominator, so PR-AUC *does* move with $\pi$. On an imbalanced problem, **report PR-AUC (average precision)**, and state the base rate next to it or the number means nothing.

A no-skill detector has ROC-AUC $0.5$ and PR-AUC $\pi$. Compare against those baselines, not against zero.

## Metrics that survive contact with operations

- **Precision@k** — you can investigate $k$ alerts a day. How many are real? This is usually the metric the business has.
- **Alert budget** — fix $k$ first, then maximise recall subject to it. Backwards from the textbook, correct in practice.
- **Recall at fixed FPR** — when the cost of a miss dominates.

## Time series needs different metrics

The **point-adjust** protocol — if any point in a true anomalous window is flagged, count the whole window as detected — is widespread and badly inflationary. Under it, random scores can beat published methods. Prefer **range-based precision and recall**, or **VUS-PR**, and always say which protocol you used.

## Shipping

- **Drift.** Normal moves. Refit on a schedule, and monitor the *flag rate* — a detector whose alert volume doubles overnight has usually detected a change in itself.
- **Seasonality and warm-up.** A weekly cycle needs weeks of history. Do not alert during warm-up.
- **Alert fatigue** is a failure mode of the system, not of the people. Deduplicate, group by root cause, and suppress known-benign patterns.
- **Human-in-the-loop.** Every dismissal is a label. Capture it. **Active learning** — asking the analyst about the points the model is most uncertain on — is the cheapest accuracy you will ever buy, and it converts an unsupervised problem into the semi-supervised one that scene 1 said was easier.
- **Explainability.** "Anomalous, score 0.87" is not actionable. Per-feature attribution on the score, and a counterfactual — *what would have to change for this to be normal* — is what makes an alert investigable.
scenes.prompt: Scene 6 of six, and the one that decides whether anything ships. The evaluation set is 400 points, 8% anomalous, with overlapping score distributions -- AUC-ROC 0.9252, average precision 0.7955, and at threshold 0.5: TP 21, FP 4, FN 11, TN 364, precision 0.840, recall 0.656, accuracy 0.963. The killer comparison: always predicting 'normal' scores 0.920 accuracy, so the detector's 0.963 is worth far less than it looks. The base-rate slider drives adPrecBayes with TPR and FPR held fixed at 0.8 and 0.05: precision is 0.582 at pi = 0.08 and 0.016 at pi = 0.001, a 37x collapse while ROC-AUC does not move at all. That non-movement is the argument against ROC-AUC on imbalanced problems, and the checker verifies the identity reproduces the measured precision exactly at every threshold. Baselines to compare against: ROC-AUC 0.5 and PR-AUC = pi for a no-skill detector. On time series, be direct that the point-adjust protocol is badly inflationary and that random scores can beat published methods under it. The operational half -- drift, warm-up, alert fatigue, human-in-the-loop labelling, explainability -- is not padding; it is where deployed detectors actually die, and the active-learning point closes the loop back to scene 1.

A detector has run. Every point has a score in $[0, 1]$, sorted here from highest to lowest, and $8\%$ of them are genuinely anomalous (red).

The two populations **overlap**. That is not a defect of this detector — it is the situation every real detector is in. If the distributions separated cleanly you would not need a threshold, you would need an `if`.

Drag the **threshold**. Everything at or above it is flagged. Notice that you are not choosing an accuracy; you are choosing a trade between two kinds of mistake, and there is no value of the threshold that avoids both.

steps.description:
The confusion matrix, live. Note the scale: **TN dominates everything**, because $92\%$ of the data is normal and most of it scores low.

That domination is what makes accuracy useless. Accuracy is $(\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{TN})/N$, and $\mathrm{TN}$ alone is already $0.92$ of $N$ if you flag nothing at all.

steps.title: ROC against PR — and why one of them lies to you
steps.description:
Both curves are the same threshold sweep, plotted in two coordinate systems. The gold dot on each is your current threshold.

**ROC** — TPR against FPR. Both axes are normalised *within* a class: TPR divides by the number of positives, FPR by the number of negatives. Neither denominator knows how many of each there are. So the ROC curve, and its area, are **completely independent of the base rate**.

That sounds like a virtue. On an imbalanced problem it is the opposite: make your problem a hundred times harder by dropping the base rate a hundredfold, and ROC-AUC will not move a single digit.

**PR** — precision against recall. Precision is $\mathrm{TP}/(\mathrm{TP} + \mathrm{FP})$, and $\mathrm{FP}$ comes from the negative class, so precision *does* feel the imbalance. The dashed level at $\pi$ is the no-skill baseline: a random scorer sits there.

Here: **ROC-AUC $= 0.925$**, which sounds excellent. **Average precision $= 0.796$** against a no-skill floor of $0.08$, which is genuinely good — but the two numbers are answering different questions, and only the second one is about your problem.

> Report **average precision, with the base rate beside it.** A PR-AUC without its $\pi$ is uninterpretable.
steps.prompt: The metric comparison. The mechanism must be precise: TPR = TP/P and FPR = FP/N, both normalised within a class, so neither knows the class ratio and the ROC curve is invariant to it. Precision = TP/(TP+FP) mixes classes, so PR is not invariant. The consequence is the recommendation: on imbalanced problems report average precision with the base rate stated beside it, because PR-AUC alone is uninterpretable without knowing the no-skill floor. Numbers here: AUC-ROC 0.9252 against a no-skill 0.5, average precision 0.7955 against a no-skill 0.08. Both curves are swept by rank so every plotted point is a genuine operating point, and the checker cross-validates AUC-ROC against the Mann-Whitney U statistic by an independent route.

add.prompt: The ROC curve, swept by rank over 120 operating points. The grey diagonal is a random scorer. The gold dot is the current threshold. The property to stress: this curve would be IDENTICAL if the base rate were 0.001 instead of 0.08, because both axes normalise within their own class. That invariance is what makes ROC-AUC the wrong headline number for a rare-event problem.

add.prompt: The precision-recall curve over the same 120 operating points. The grey horizontal line at 0.08 is the no-skill floor -- a random scorer's precision equals the base rate at every recall. Average precision here is 0.7955, so the detector is well clear of the floor. Unlike ROC, this whole picture would move if the base rate changed, which is the reason to prefer it.

steps.title: The base rate, and the detector that stops working without changing
steps.description:
Now the slider that matters. **$\pi$** is the true fraction of anomalies in the population — a fact about the world, not about your model.

Hold **a** detector completely fixed at $\mathrm{TPR} = 0.8$, $\mathrm{FPR} = 0.05$ and slide $\pi$ down from $0.2$. *(Those are round numbers for a good detector, not this page's one — this dataset's detector reaches $\mathrm{TPR} = 0.81$ only at $\mathrm{FPR} = 0.14$. The argument does not depend on which detector it is.)*

$$\mathrm{precision} = \frac{0.8\,\pi}{0.8\,\pi + 0.05(1-\pi)}$$

| $\pi$ | precision | of every 100 alerts, real |
|---|---|---|
| $0.20$ | $0.800$ | 80 |
| $0.08$ | $0.582$ | 58 |
| $0.01$ | $0.139$ | 14 |
| $0.001$ | $0.016$ | **1.6** |

At $\pi = 0.001$ — an *optimistic* rate for fraud, intrusion or hardware failure — this detector produces **62 false alarms for every real one**. Nobody will keep reading them, and they are right not to.

And the model did not change. Its ROC curve is exactly where it was; its ROC-AUC has not moved a digit. Every metric that normalises within a class is blind to what just happened.

## What to do about it

Only two levers exist, and neither is "train longer".

1. **Drive FPR down, hard.** Precision at low $\pi$ is governed almost entirely by $\mathrm{FPR}\cdot(1-\pi)$. Halving FPR roughly doubles precision; raising TPR from $0.8$ to $0.9$ buys you almost nothing.
2. **Raise the effective base rate.** Segment, filter, or restrict to the population where anomalies actually live. Going from "all traffic" to "traffic from new accounts in the first hour" may move $\pi$ by two orders of magnitude, and that is worth more than any model you could train.
steps.prompt: The scene's punchline and the lesson's. Hold TPR = 0.8 and FPR = 0.05 fixed and slide pi: precision is 0.800 at pi = 0.2, 0.582 at 0.08, 0.139 at 0.01 and 0.016 at 0.001. At the last one, 62 false alarms per true one. The model has not changed and its ROC-AUC has not moved -- that is the demonstration, not an aside. The two levers are the actionable content and the student should leave able to state them: drive FPR down (precision at low pi is dominated by FPR(1-pi), so halving FPR roughly doubles precision while raising TPR from 0.8 to 0.9 buys almost nothing), and raise the effective base rate by segmenting the population (all traffic versus new accounts in their first hour can move pi by two orders of magnitude, which beats any training run). This is the same Bayes computation as the medical-test problem in the Conditional Probability lesson; say so, the connection is worth making.

steps.title: Shipping: the problems no metric shows you
steps.description:
Everything above assumed a fixed labelled dataset. Production has none of those things.

**Drift.** Normal moves — releases, seasons, product changes, the business growing. A detector fitted last quarter is measuring last quarter. Refit on a schedule, and **monitor the flag rate as a first-class signal**: a detector whose alert volume doubles overnight has usually detected a change in itself, not in the world.

**Warm-up and seasonality.** A weekly cycle needs several weeks of history before the model knows what a Tuesday looks like. Do not alert during warm-up; you will train your users to ignore you in week one.

**Alert fatigue is a system failure, not a people failure.** Deduplicate. Group by probable root cause. Suppress known-benign patterns explicitly, and *review the suppression list* — it is where real incidents go to hide. Fix the alert budget first, and tune to it.

**Human-in-the-loop.** Every dismissal is a label, and almost every deployment throws them away. Capture them. **Active learning** — asking the analyst about the points the model is least certain of — is the cheapest accuracy available anywhere in this lesson, and it converts your unsupervised problem into the semi-supervised one scene 1 said was easier. The loop closes.

**Explainability.** *"Anomalous, score 0.87"* is not an alert, it is a riddle. What makes an alert actionable:
- **which features** drove the score (per-feature attribution — Shapley values on the score work, and for an Isolation Forest the split features on the short paths are nearly free);
- **what normal looked like** for this entity at this time;
- a **counterfactual** — *what would have had to be different for this not to fire*.

## The whole lesson, in six lines

1. Define which kind of anomaly you have before choosing a method. *(1)*
2. Use robust estimators; check the breakdown point. *(2)*
3. Make the score **relative** to local structure, and whiten correlated axes. *(3)*
4. Isolation Forest is the strongest cheap default; $\nu$ lets you state your alert budget. *(4)*
5. Deep methods earn their place through better **representations**, and die of the capacity trap. *(5)*
6. Report **average precision with the base rate beside it**, chase **FPR**, and capture every label a human gives you. *(6)*

And the sentence to keep: **a detector is a ranking; the threshold is a decision; the base rate decides whether that decision is worth making.**
steps.prompt: The closing step. This is where deployed detectors actually die, so do not let it read as a checklist. Drift: monitor the FLAG RATE as a first-class signal, because a doubling of alert volume usually means the detector changed, not the world. Warm-up: alerting before the model knows what a Tuesday looks like trains users to ignore you permanently. Alert fatigue: a system failure, and the suppression list is where real incidents hide, so it needs reviewing. Human-in-the-loop: every dismissal is a label and almost everyone discards them; active learning on the model's least certain points is the cheapest accuracy in the whole lesson and it closes the loop back to scene 1's claim that a little supervision beats a lot of architecture. Explainability: name the three things that make an alert actionable -- which features drove it, what normal looked like for this entity at this time, and a counterfactual. Note that for an Isolation Forest the split features along short paths give attribution nearly free. The six-line summary is the lesson's spine; the final sentence is what a student should be able to repeat a month later.

proof.title: Bayes: precision is not a property of your detector
proof.techniqueHint: Bayes' theorem, with the class-conditional rates the detector actually controls on one side and the base rate on the other.
proof.goal: Derive $\mathrm{precision} = \dfrac{\mathrm{TPR}\,\pi}{\mathrm{TPR}\,\pi + \mathrm{FPR}(1-\pi)}$ and show that it vanishes as $\pi \to 0$ for any fixed detector with $\mathrm{FPR} > 0$.
proof.prompt: The proof behind the scene's punchline, and the same computation as the medical-test problem in the Conditional Probability lesson -- make the link explicitly, because a student who has seen that one already has this. The structure is: TPR and FPR are CONDITIONAL on the true class and are therefore properties of the detector; precision conditions the other way and therefore needs the prior. The limit in the final step is the operational fact: for any fixed detector with FPR > 0, precision tends to zero as the base rate does, at rate TPR*pi/FPR. The corollary about which lever to pull is the actionable part: d(precision)/d(FPR) dominates d(precision)/d(TPR) at small pi, so halving FPR roughly doubles precision while improving TPR barely registers.

steps.explanation: Two sources of alerts: the real ones, and the false ones. The second term is multiplied by $(1 - \pi)$, which is *almost all of the data* when anomalies are rare — and that is the whole problem in one term.

steps.label: Invert the conditioning
steps.justification: Bayes' theorem, with the denominator from the previous line.
steps.explanation: Precision conditions on **the alert**, not on the truth — so unlike TPR and FPR it cannot be computed without the prior. This is the identical computation to the medical-test problem: a test with excellent sensitivity and specificity still produces mostly false positives when the disease is rare.

nodes.subexpr: T P R \pi + F P R{\left(1 - \pi \right)}

steps.label: Take the base rate to zero
steps.justification: For fixed $\mathrm{FPR} > 0$ the numerator is $O(\pi)$ while the denominator tends to $\mathrm{FPR}$, so the ratio is asymptotically linear in $\pi$ with slope $\mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR}$.
steps.explanation: So precision falls to zero **for every detector that ever produces a false positive**, no matter how good it is, as the problem gets rarer. No amount of training prevents this; it is arithmetic.

steps.label: Which lever to pull
steps.justification: Differentiating the identity in $\mathrm{TPR}$ and in $\mathrm{FPR}$ and taking the ratio; the common denominator cancels.
steps.explanation: The base rate cancels: the trade is set by **where you sit on the ROC curve**, not by how rare the anomaly is. At $\mathrm{TPR} = 0.80$ and $\mathrm{FPR} = 0.01$ the ratio is $-80$ — one absolute point of $\mathrm{FPR}$ costs eighty times what the same point of $\mathrm{TPR}$ buys. **Chase false positives, not recall.** $\pi$ enters one step earlier, through $\text{precision} \sim (\mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR})\,\pi$: you cannot change the trade-off, but you *can* change $\pi$ by narrowing the population you score. Going from "all traffic" to "new accounts in their first hour" can move the base rate by two orders of magnitude, which is more than any model will give you.
